questions.q: Why does this lesson say a project's README and diagram matter more than exhaustive inline code comments for a portfolio review?
options: A hiring manager typically spends minutes, not hours, on any one project — often just skimming the README and one diagram before deciding whether to look closer
Code comments are actively harmful to a portfolio
Reviewers always read every file in the repository in full
READMEs are required by industry regulation
questions.explain: This changes what's worth polishing — making sure the short time a reviewer spends lands on the decisions that matter.

questions.q: What four questions should a project's README answer, in order, according to this lesson?
options: What the system does, what it looks like, what the hard decisions were, and how to run it
Who wrote it, when it was written, what license it uses, and its file count
The full commit history, in chronological order
Every configuration setting used in the project
questions.explain: This order puts the scenario and architecture up front, then the honest reasoning, then proof the system actually runs.

questions.q: Where does this lesson say the README's "hard decisions" section should come from?
options: Directly from the project's written retrospective — the honest, specific answer to "what would you change"
A freshly invented explanation written just for the portfolio
The original project requirements document
A generic list of best practices unrelated to the specific project
questions.explain: The retrospectives from Lessons 74 and 78 are the direct source, because they already contain specific, honest answers a resume bullet can't convey.

questions.q: What is the "sufficiency test" this lesson proposes for an architecture diagram?
options: Whether someone who never took the course could understand the system's shape from the diagram alone, in under a minute
Whether the diagram includes every table column and configuration setting
Whether the diagram is at least one full page long
Whether the diagram uses the exact same tool as every other project
questions.explain: A good diagram is five or six boxes and arrows — the system's shape, not exhaustive technical detail.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the three capstone projects together as "a deliberately wide range" for a portfolio?
options: They cover batch, migration, and streaming work — different shapes of system, rather than three variations on the same idea
They were built using three completely unrelated technology stacks with no shared concepts
Each project uses a different programming language
Portfolio reviewers only look at the most recent project
questions.explain: The retail platform, warehouse migration, and fraud detector give a reviewer three genuinely different kinds of systems to sample from.
